question: Does antiretroviral therapy reduce HIV transmission and tuberculosis?
answer: Yes. Large‐scale trials have shown that early antiretroviral therapy (ART) cuts sexual HIV transmission by more than 95 %; in the HPTN 052 study, transmission to seronegative partners was 0.3 % in the treated arm versus 2.8 % in the delayed‑treatment arm (hazard ratio 0.04), and the PARTNER and PARTNER 2 studies reported zero linked transmissions after 77 000 condom‑less sex acts among virally suppressed couples. The same viral suppression that prevents HIV spread also lowers the risk of active tuberculosis (TB) in people living with HIV, with cohort analyses indicating a roughly 50 % reduction in TB incidence when CD4 counts are maintained above 350 cells/µL on ART. A 2013 WHO meta‑analysis of 13 studies found the pooled TB incidence rate fell from 7.5 to 3.2 cases per 100 person‑years after ART initiation. Moreover, universal “treat‑all” policies have been linked to declines in national TB notification rates among HIV‑positive populations, such as a 31 % drop in South Africa between 2010 and 2016. These data demonstrate that ART is a powerful tool for both preventing HIV transmission and curbing TB disease in infected individuals.
